summary:
Recommendation: move the MySQL wordpress database to three AWS services in three waves, with the target schemas designed for each. Wave 1 moves it to Aurora MySQL, which serves 62.6% of the queries. Wave 2 puts ElastiCache in front of 15 hot reads, which carry 77.5% of calls. Wave 3 moves the key-value and point-lookup queries, 37.4% of the workload, to DynamoDB. The projected cost of the full modernization is $513 per month at AWS Price List on-demand prices for us-east-1, retrieved 2026-10-25. No current cost was collected for the source database, so the plan claims no saving against it.

Risk: overall risk is medium. Two exposures drive it: reads on DynamoDB that depend on change data capture (CDC) to stay in sync, and queries where two engines scored almost the same. Before wave 3 starts, set up and test the CDC replication and confirm where those queries run.

Decision: approve wave 1. It moves the database 1:1 to Aurora MySQL, the same engine family as MySQL, with its current data model, and its cutover waits until schema and data parity is validated against the source.

Schema design produced 49 target objects: 107 queries in 59 query groups; 115 in-scope access patterns (Aurora MySQL: 20 target tables, 67 in-scope access patterns; DynamoDB: 17 target tables, 35 in-scope access patterns; ElastiCache: 12 key designs, 13 in-scope access patterns). risks.description: [elasticache] The cache design marks 5 patterns unsupported; the engineering report lists each one with its workaround under Target schemas by engine.
details: unsupported pattern: Query `52da34b1` filters posts by post_type, an exact post_title and a status list, sorted by post_date_gmt with a row limit. It returns no rows in the sample and the filter combination has no stable key. Workaround: Keep this lookup on the owner database, which serves it from its own indexes

unsupported pattern: Query `06584926` selects the next scheduled actions by hook and status ordered by scheduled date. Its result changes with every status transition of the action queue, so a cached copy gives a wrong queue head. Workaround: Keep the queue selection on the owner database

unsupported pattern: Query `d4bf16d6` is a paginated post listing with a total row count (SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS), ordered by date. Every page offset and status value would need its own key, and any post write changes the totals. Workaround: Keep paginated listings on the owner database

unsupported pattern: Query `f31a66f5` lists child posts of a parent with an OR across eight statuses ordered by date. The status combinations make the key space large and any post write alters the lists. Workaround: Keep the child post listing on the owner database

unsupported pattern: Query `fcfd82fa` is a slug uniqueness check that excludes the post being saved. A stale cached answer could allow a duplicate slug, so the check must read current data. Workaround: Keep the uniqueness check on the owner database, which enforces it with current rows
risks.mitigation: Serve these patterns from their owner engine or add them to the cache design before the Wave 2 gate, as the design's workaround for each says.

risks.description: [dynamodb] The DynamoDB schema design records 23 trade-offs to review, listed under Migration trade-offs in the engineering report.
details: Comment and log ids that MySQL assigned with AUTO_INCREMENT (`comment_ID`, `log_id`) become application-generated numeric ids written with an `attribute_not_exists` condition
Comment meta rows (query `65f7884e`) are an identifying relationship keyed by `comment_id` with sort key `meta_id`, and the IN list becomes one Query per comment_id

No GSI is designed: the source indexes on post_author, post_name, post_parent, user_login, user_email, user_nicename, status, hook and scheduled_date_gmt serve no query in this part, and no unique non-key attribute is written by an in-scope query
Posts and their meta rows share one item collection in `wp_posts`, keyed by post_id, with the post stored at SK `POST` and each meta row at SK `META#<meta_key>#<meta_id>`

Queries `2c0093ed` and `33dfdb12` add to or subtract from meta_value, a text column, in one UPDATE; DynamoDB stores meta_value as a string, so the application reads the value, computes the new one and writes it
Query `3440484f` filters a post by ID and post_type; the ID alone addresses one item, so it is a GetItem and the application checks post_type on the returned item

Query `50b46567` reads `wp_termmeta` for a list of term IDs and was flagged for full scans (7,741); it becomes one Query on PK=term_id per ID, and the ORDER BY meta_id is applied by the application because the sort key starts with meta_key

TEXT and LONGTEXT columns stay inline: `wp_posts` averages 711 bytes per item (post_content, post_title, post_excerpt, post_content_filtered, to_ping and pinged are capped columns), `wp_postmeta` 144 bytes (meta_value), `wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta` 131 bytes (meta_value) and `wp_actionscheduler_actions` 587 bytes (schedule, extended_args), against the 400 KB item limit. `wp_users` holds 1 row, so its measured size reflects page overhead and the schema-based estimate of 1,245 bytes is used

The API key lookup by `consumer_key` (query `1794daed`) reads the `ApiKeysByConsumerKey` index, which projects `user_id`, `permissions`, `consumer_secret` and `nonces`; the `last_access` update (query `0452bed2`, 248.3 writes per second at design load) writes only the base item

The approved-comment count of a post (query `8c66eaee`) is a Query with Select=COUNT on the `CommentsByPostApproval` index, keyed by post and approval status; the source examines 2.42 rows per call on average
The autoload read (query `413c99e4`) is served by the OptionsByAutoload index with partition key autoload, which holds almost every item under one key value, and projects option_value

The meta tables (`wp_postmeta`, `wp_termmeta`, `wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta`) allow several rows with the same meta_key under one parent, so each sort key ends with meta_id and the update by parent id and meta_key (queries `ea7778db`, `2c0093ed`, `33dfdb12`, `3c5c8a79`, `4b856e29`) is a Query on `begins_with '<meta_key>#'` followed by an UpdateItem
The option update (query `ac34da34`) carries the condition attribute_exists(option_name)

The set-based writes by `order_id` become key-scoped operations: the reserved stock release (query `77cd1ad7`) is a Query on the table's partition key `order_id` plus BatchWriteItem deletes, and the permission reassignment (query `2264704d`) is a Query on the `PermissionsByOrder` index followed by one UpdateItem per returned item

The source IDs (post ID, meta_id, order_item_id, action_id) are AUTO_INCREMENT; DynamoDB has no sequence, so the application generates each new numeric ID before the PutItem, and every insert carries `attribute_not_exists` on the partition key

The tax rate class list (query `329367a2`, a full read of a 2-row table) becomes one Query on a constant partition key `tax_rate_scope`, with the sort key `name_key` (name#tax_rate_class_id) giving name order
`comment_content` (table average row of 552 bytes), `meta_value` (commentmeta estimated average of 52429 bytes) and `nonces` (API keys estimated average of 52429 bytes) stay inline in their items
option_value stays inline in the item instead of moving to S3
wp_options is keyed by option_name, the unique column every lookup, update and delete uses, instead of the auto-increment option_id

wp_term_relationships has no GSI on term_taxonomy_id and wp_woocommerce_order_items has none on order_id: the only queries in this part (query `0d20f1d9` and query `674ead2f`) address them by full primary key

wp_usermeta is keyed by user_id with umeta_id as sort key, so one Query per user returns that user's meta rows in the source ORDER BY umeta_id order. The IN list of query `3a74580e` becomes parallel Queries, one per user_id
wp_usermeta.meta_value (longtext) stays inline in the item: the table's avg_row_size_bytes is 16478 against the 400 KB item limit, and query `3a74580e` returns the value on every read

wp_woocommerce_order_items.order_item_id is an auto-increment column in the source; DynamoDB has no sequence, so the application assigns the id and the insert (query `674ead2f`) carries attribute_not_exists(order_item_id)

trade_offs.description: The schema is carried over from MySQL with column types unchanged. The changes are three index edits on wp_postmeta, wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta and wp_posts, plus recommendations for a read replica and an application object cache.
trade_offs.impact: Application code and plugins keep working without changes, which keeps migration risk low. The cost is that the WordPress metadata tables stay in the key-value layout that causes most of the row reads, so the gain comes from indexes and caching and not from a new data model.

trade_offs.description: WooCommerce reporting queries (`a0b655ea`, `fc99562b`) aggregate over wp_posts and the metadata tables with joins that examine tens to hundreds of thousands of rows per call. They stay in Aurora MySQL and move to a replica, and no index is added for them.
trade_offs.impact: These queries run about once every 33 seconds and take 0.2 to 0.9 seconds each. Running them on a replica keeps them off the writer, but they stay the slowest queries in the workload until the application changes how it stores order totals.

trade_offs.description: Comment and log ids that MySQL assigned with AUTO_INCREMENT (`comment_ID`, `log_id`) become application-generated numeric ids written with an `attribute_not_exists` condition.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB has no auto-increment column, so the WordPress and Action Scheduler code that inserts these rows (queries `de9a7ba3` and `b05af520`) must generate a unique id before each PutItem; a duplicate id fails the write instead of overwriting a row.

trade_offs.description: The approved-comment count of a post (query `8c66eaee`) is a Query with Select=COUNT on the `CommentsByPostApproval` index, keyed by post and approval status; the source examines 2.42 rows per call on average.
trade_offs.impact: The count reads and bills every matching index entry (keys only, so each page is small) instead of an index scan in MySQL. With 29651 comments spread over many posts the per-post collections stay small, so no counter item is kept; a post with a very large comment collection would need an atomic counter item updated in the same transaction as the comment write. The index lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a count that must include a comment just inserted reads after that write is applied.

trade_offs.description: `comment_content` (table average row of 552 bytes), `meta_value` (commentmeta estimated average of 52429 bytes) and `nonces` (API keys estimated average of 52429 bytes) stay inline in their items.
trade_offs.impact: Each average sits far under the 400 KB item limit, so no S3 pointer attribute is used. A single value above 400 KB cannot be stored: the migration load rejects such a row and it moves to S3 with a pointer attribute.

trade_offs.description: The tax rate class list (query `329367a2`, a full read of a 2-row table) becomes one Query on a constant partition key `tax_rate_scope`, with the sort key `name_key` (name#tax_rate_class_id) giving name order.
trade_offs.impact: All rows live in one item collection, so the 37.9 reads per second are one Query of about 433 bytes per item against the 3000 RCU/s partition limit, and no Scan runs. The rows change rarely; the application can also cache the list. The unique `slug` constraint has no in-scope writer, so no sentinel item is written.

trade_offs.description: The API key lookup by `consumer_key` (query `1794daed`) reads the `ApiKeysByConsumerKey` index, which projects `user_id`, `permissions`, `consumer_secret` and `nonces`; the `last_access` update (query `0452bed2`, 248.3 writes per second at design load) writes only the base item.
trade_offs.impact: Review this trade-off with the DynamoDB schema design before migration.

trade_offs.description: The set-based writes by `order_id` become key-scoped operations: the reserved stock release (query `77cd1ad7`) is a Query on the table's partition key `order_id` plus BatchWriteItem deletes, and the permission reassignment (query `2264704d`) is a Query on the `PermissionsByOrder` index followed by one UpdateItem per returned item.
trade_offs.impact: A single SQL statement becomes a Query plus one write per item and is no longer atomic across the order's items; the application retries items that fail. `PermissionsByOrder` is keys only and does not carry `user_id` or `user_email`, so the updates cause no index writes. The index lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it.

trade_offs.description: Comment meta rows (query `65f7884e`) are an identifying relationship keyed by `comment_id` with sort key `meta_id`, and the IN list becomes one Query per comment_id.
trade_offs.impact: A page that loads meta for N comments issues N Queries, which the application can send in parallel; `wp_commentmeta` is empty today, so the load is 1.5 Queries per second at design load.

trade_offs.description: Posts and their meta rows share one item collection in `wp_posts`, keyed by post_id, with the post stored at SK `POST` and each meta row at SK `META#<meta_key>#<meta_id>`.

The ID-list reads (queries `a16f38a0` and `0e169d06`) become BatchGetItem calls of up to 100 keys. trade_offs.description: The meta tables (`wp_postmeta`, `wp_termmeta`, `wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta`) allow several rows with the same meta_key under one parent, so each sort key ends with meta_id and the update by parent id and meta_key (queries `ea7778db`, `2c0093ed`, `33dfdb12`, `3c5c8a79`, `4b856e29`) is a Query on `begins_with '<meta_key>#'` followed by an UpdateItem.

The write itself is conditional on the item existing, which matches the source UPDATE touching no row when none matches.

trade_offs.description: Queries `2c0093ed` and `33dfdb12` add to or subtract from meta_value, a text column, in one UPDATE; DynamoDB stores meta_value as a string, so the application reads the value, computes the new one and writes it.
trade_offs.impact: Two concurrent adjustments to the same meta item can overwrite each other, where MySQL applied both under its row lock. The observed rate is 5.3 writes per second for each of the two queries at design load across all items. A meta key that the application uses as a counter moves to a numeric attribute updated with an atomic `ADD` before cutover.

trade_offs.description: The source IDs (post ID, meta_id, order_item_id, action_id) are AUTO_INCREMENT; DynamoDB has no sequence, so the application generates each new numeric ID before the PutItem, and every insert carries `attribute_not_exists` on the partition key.
trade_offs.impact: Migrated rows keep their source IDs. trade_offs.description: Query `50b46567` reads `wp_termmeta` for a list of term IDs and was flagged for full scans (7,741); it becomes one Query on PK=term_id per ID, and the ORDER BY meta_id is applied by the application because the sort key starts with meta_key.

trade_offs.description: Query `3440484f` filters a post by ID and post_type; the ID alone addresses one item, so it is a GetItem and the application checks post_type on the returned item.
trade_offs.impact: A request for an ID with a different post_type reads the item and discards it. The ID is unique, so at most one item is read per call, at 1.9 calls per second at design load.

trade_offs.description: TEXT and LONGTEXT columns stay inline: `wp_posts` averages 711 bytes per item (post_content, post_title, post_excerpt, post_content_filtered, to_ping and pinged are capped columns), `wp_postmeta` 144 bytes (meta_value), `wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta` 131 bytes (meta_value) and `wp_actionscheduler_actions` 587 bytes (schedule, extended_args), against the 400 KB item limit. `wp_users` holds 1 row, so its measured size reflects page overhead and the schema-based estimate of 1,245 bytes is used.
trade_offs.impact: No item needs an S3 pointer at the measured sizes. A post or meta value that grows past 400 KB is rejected by DynamoDB and moves to S3 with a pointer attribute.

trade_offs.description: No GSI is designed: the source indexes on post_author, post_name, post_parent, user_login, user_email, user_nicename, status, hook and scheduled_date_gmt serve no query in this part, and no unique non-key attribute is written by an in-scope query.
trade_offs.impact: A lookup by post name, author, user login, user email or action status has no access path in this design. When such a query is added, it gets a GSI on that attribute then. Zero dates (`0000-00-00 00:00:00`) in datetime columns are not valid ISO 8601 and are omitted from the migrated item.

trade_offs.description: wp_woocommerce_order_items.order_item_id is an auto-increment column in the source; DynamoDB has no sequence, so the application assigns the id and the insert (query `674ead2f`) carries attribute_not_exists(order_item_id).
trade_offs.impact: Existing ids migrate unchanged. New ids come from an application-side numeric generator, and an id collision rejects the write instead of overwriting an order item.

trade_offs.description: wp_usermeta is keyed by user_id with umeta_id as sort key, so one Query per user returns that user's meta rows in the source ORDER BY umeta_id order. The IN list of query `3a74580e` becomes parallel Queries, one per user_id.
trade_offs.impact: The application issues one Query per user in the list instead of a single IN statement; each Query reads one partition, and the sort key keeps the original row order.

trade_offs.description: wp_usermeta.meta_value (longtext) stays inline in the item: the table's avg_row_size_bytes is 16478 against the 400 KB item limit, and query `3a74580e` returns the value on every read.
trade_offs.impact: Items stay far below the item limit at the measured average. A single value that approaches 400 KB would need to move to S3 with a pointer attribute; the migration checks the largest meta_value before load.

trade_offs.description: wp_term_relationships has no GSI on term_taxonomy_id and wp_woocommerce_order_items has none on order_id: the only queries in this part (query `0d20f1d9` and query `674ead2f`) address them by full primary key.
trade_offs.impact: The source secondary indexes on these columns are not carried over, which saves their write and storage cost. A read by term or by order added later needs a GSI at that time.

trade_offs.description: wp_options is keyed by option_name, the unique column every lookup, update and delete uses, instead of the auto-increment option_id.
trade_offs.impact: Single-option reads and writes are one GetItem, UpdateItem, PutItem or DeleteItem call by name. The unique index on option_name needs no sentinel item because the name is the table key, so a duplicate name is an overwrite, as in the source ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE. option_id stays as a plain attribute and nothing queries it.

trade_offs.description: The autoload read (query `413c99e4`) is served by the OptionsByAutoload index with partition key autoload, which holds almost every item under one key value, and projects option_value.
trade_offs.impact: One Query returns about 247 items per call, so the index partition for the value yes carries about 1,726 read units per second at design load, 58% of the 3,000 limit, and every value update, insert and delete is written to the index as well, about 258 write units per second, 26% of the 1,000 limit. Sharding the autoload value is not needed at this load; it is needed if the read rate grows beyond the 10x design multiplier.

trade_offs.description: option_value stays inline in the item instead of moving to S3.
trade_offs.impact: The table's average row size is 360 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, so one option fits in an item. A single value above 400 KB (a very large serialized option) is stored in S3 with a pointer attribute written by the application; the migration checks the largest option_value before load.

trade_offs.description: The option update (query `ac34da34`) carries the condition attribute_exists(option_name).
trade_offs.impact: The source UPDATE changes zero rows when the option is missing; an unconditional UpdateItem would create the item instead. The condition keeps the source behaviour and a missing option returns a conditional check failure that the application treats as no rows affected.

trade_offs.description: Options are cached as one hash per option name with a one-hour TTL.
trade_offs.impact: After a settings change the cached option stays until the application deletes its key, and for at most the one-hour TTL if that delete fails. A read that must see the change at once reads the owner database, which serves every cache miss.

trade_offs.description: Meta rows are stored as one JSON array per parent id instead of one key per meta row.
trade_offs.impact: A read costs one GET or one MGET for the whole set, but any single meta change rewrites the whole array, so the write path deletes the key and the next read refills it. The postmeta and key_ids copies hold the same data twice, which adds roughly 50% memory for those keys.

trade_offs.description: Term join results are denormalized into per-object term id lists with a 15-minute TTL.
trade_offs.impact: A term assignment change is not visible in the cache until the list expires, at most 15 minutes. No observed write covers term relationships, so a read that must see the change at once reads the owner database.

trade_offs.description: Action scheduler rows are cached with a 120-second TTL, and queue selection and slug uniqueness checks stay on the owner database.
trade_offs.impact: A cached action shows an old status for at most 120 seconds after a transition. Queries `06584926` and `fcfd82fa` and the other listing queries are not cached, so their load stays on the owner database.

unsupported_patterns.reason: Query `52da34b1` filters posts by post_type, an exact post_title and a status list, sorted by post_date_gmt with a row limit. It returns no rows in the sample and the filter combination has no stable key.
unsupported_patterns.workaround: Keep this lookup on the owner database, which serves it from its own indexes.

unsupported_patterns.reason: Query `06584926` selects the next scheduled actions by hook and status ordered by scheduled date. Its result changes with every status transition of the action queue, so a cached copy gives a wrong queue head.
unsupported_patterns.workaround: Keep the queue selection on the owner database.

unsupported_patterns.reason: Query `d4bf16d6` is a paginated post listing with a total row count (SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS), ordered by date. Every page offset and status value would need its own key, and any post write changes the totals.
unsupported_patterns.workaround: Keep paginated listings on the owner database.

unsupported_patterns.reason: Query `f31a66f5` lists child posts of a parent with an OR across eight statuses ordered by date. The status combinations make the key space large and any post write alters the lists.
unsupported_patterns.workaround: Keep the child post listing on the owner database.

unsupported_patterns.reason: Query `fcfd82fa` is a slug uniqueness check that excludes the post being saved. A stale cached answer could allow a duplicate slug, so the check must read current data.
unsupported_patterns.workaround: Keep the uniqueness check on the owner database, which enforces it with current rows.

migration_notes.application_logic_required: On a miss the application reads the owner database, writes the key with its TTL and returns the result. After each owner write commits, the application deletes the affected keys listed in the cache invalidation plan.

migration_waves.title: Move to Aurora MySQL
migration_waves.rationale: The whole source database (MySQL 8.0.45) moves 1:1 to Aurora MySQL: same engine family. The collector reports engine and version only; feature compatibility is not assessed here. 67 queries (62.6%) remain on Aurora MySQL once later waves have moved their share; later waves move subsets of these 50 tables and views out of Aurora MySQL. 22 of these tables and views are mapped to a target engine in the migration map; later waves move 15 of the 50 off Aurora MySQL, and the other 35 stay on Aurora MySQL.

migration_waves.title: Cache hot reads with ElastiCache
migration_waves.rationale: 15 hot reads (77.5% of calls), cache-aside in front of Aurora MySQL in wave 2, then DynamoDB once wave 3 moves these reads: no data migration, fully reversible. It takes the read pressure off before the data migrations that follow. These reads belong to queries that move in wave 1 (Aurora MySQL) and wave 3 (DynamoDB); this share overlaps the owner shares, which alone sum to 100%.
